lesson.title: Congress Takes Control: The Radical Reconstruction of the South
lesson.summary: Furious at Andrew Johnson's lenient policies and the Black Codes they produced, Congress seized control of Reconstruction in 1867, placing the South under military rule and, for a brief period, opening real political power to Black Southerners.
lesson.body:
Congress's rejection of Andrew Johnson's Reconstruction plan in December 1865 was only the opening move in a much larger power struggle. Throughout 1866, Republicans and Johnson battled openly. Congress passed the Civil Rights Act of 1866 over his veto and sent the Fourteenth Amendment to the states, while Johnson toured the country attacking Republican leaders in a disastrous speaking campaign that came to be called the swing around the circle. Voters responded in the 1866 midterm elections by handing Republicans veto proof majorities in both houses of Congress, a mandate the party used to take Reconstruction policy entirely out of the president's hands.

The result was the Reconstruction Act of 1867, passed on March 2, 1867, along with several follow up acts that year. The law divided the former Confederate states, except Tennessee which had already been readmitted, into five military districts, each commanded by a Union general with authority to maintain order and oversee the writing of new state constitutions. To be readmitted to the Union, each state now had to draft a constitution guaranteeing Black men the right to vote, and had to ratify the Fourteenth Amendment. This was a far more sweeping demand than anything in Lincoln's or Johnson's plans, and it placed the machinery of Southern government under direct federal military supervision for the first time.

Johnson fought the new policy at every turn, and the conflict nearly ended his presidency. When he tried to remove Secretary of War Edwin Stanton, a Republican holdover who supported the military districts, he appeared to violate the newly passed Tenure of Office Act, which required Senate approval for such removals. The House impeached Johnson in February 1868, and his Senate trial came down to a single vote in May 1868, when the Senate fell one vote short of the two thirds needed to convict and remove him. Johnson finished his term deeply weakened, and the episode showed both how far Congress was willing to go to control Reconstruction and how difficult removing a sitting president actually was.

With Johnson sidelined and Ulysses S. Grant elected president in 1868, Radical Reconstruction produced something genuinely new in American life: significant Black political power. Black men voted in large numbers across the South, and hundreds won seats in state legislatures. In 1870, Mississippi's legislature elected Hiram Revels to the United States Senate, making him the first Black member of Congress in American history, and Mississippi later sent Blanche K. Bruce to the Senate as well. These Reconstruction governments built the South's first public school systems, funded infrastructure, and expanded civil rights in state law, real and lasting achievements built by a coalition of Black voters and their white allies.

That achievement provoked ferocious resistance. Every gain Black Southerners made under Radical Reconstruction, from the ballot box to the schoolhouse, threatened a social order that many white Southerners were willing to defend through violence, and the organized backlash to Reconstruction's gains would grow alongside them throughout this same period.
